 {"list":[{"chapter_code":"JDG01","exceeding":[{"verses":"14","findings":[{"word":"לָּֽךְ׃","parsing":"Preposition | second person feminine singular","term":"perfect","elsewhere":[],"explain":"The small joining word meaning to, or for, with an ending meaning you, where you are a woman. Wilt thou. And the whole question is two little words with no verb in them at all: what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter with you, or what is it to you — the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father seeing his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him and knowing perfectly well that something is coming. Ten things worth carrying out of this verse. First, the verse opens with the same word this book opened with — and it was, after the death of Joshua — which Hebrew uses as a doorway into a scene. There is no it in the Hebrew at all; the verb stands by itself and what follows is what was. Second, and worth carrying: Hebrew has no when-word for a thing like this. It turns the verb into a naming word, puts in on the front and whose on the end, and says in her coming. And she is the one who comes: up to this verse she has been handed from one man to another as an object in a sentence, and here she arrives under her own verb. Third, and worth carrying hardest: and she urged him is the first verb in the whole book with a woman behind it. Fourth, that verb is strong — not asked and not suggested, but the word for egging somebody on, stirring them to do a thing they were not going to do, and elsewhere in the Bible it is usually a push toward something bad. Here it is a young woman getting more land out of her father, and the Bible uses the hard word without apologising for her. Who she urged is argued over, because Hebrew only says him; most take it to be her new husband, who is then to do the asking. Fifth, and worth carrying: the chapter turns back on itself. The very first thing in this book was that the sons of Israel asked — this same verb, its first appearance — asking God who should go up first. Now the word comes back for a girl asking her father for a piece of ground. It is the verb for asking and for requesting, one word for both, which is where the king called Saul got his name. Sixth, what she wants is a field: open country, ground you can plough, the word in the field where Cain killed his brother and the field Boaz owned. Not treasure, not jewellery. Land. Seventh, and worth carrying: getting down off the donkey is one of the rarest words in the Bible — three times in the whole of it, and all three times a woman getting off a donkey to ask a man for something. This verse, the same story in the book before, and years later Abigail sliding off hers in front of David. Hebrew seems to have kept one special word for exactly that movement. Eighth, a donkey is what people rode in peacetime and what carried the sacks, while a horse in these books nearly always means war. So she came out on the ordinary animal and got off it on purpose, which in that country was how you showed you were serious. Ninth, a run has just broken: up to now every voice in this chapter spoke once and never again — the people, God, Judah, a Canaanite king, Caleb. Here Caleb speaks a second time, the first person in the book to do so, twice out of six speeches, and both times handing something over. It is also the first time in the book anybody has spoken to a woman. Tenth, and worth carrying: the question is two little words with no verb in them at all — what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter, or what is it to you; the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father watching his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him, knowing perfectly well that something is coming. It is the chapter's second question, and the first one was put to God.  {"list":[{"chapter_code":"JDG01","exceeding":[{"verses":"14","findings":[{"word":"לָּֽךְ׃","parsing":"Preposition | second person feminine singular","term":"perfect","elsewhere":[],"explain":"The small joining word meaning to, or for, with an ending meaning you, where you are a woman. Wilt thou. And the whole question is two little words with no verb in them at all: what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter with you, or what is it to you — the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father seeing his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him and knowing perfectly well that something is coming. Ten things worth carrying out of this verse. First, the verse opens with the same word this book opened with — and it was, after the death of Joshua — which Hebrew uses as a doorway into a scene. There is no it in the Hebrew at all; the verb stands by itself and what follows is what was. Second, and worth carrying: Hebrew has no when-word for a thing like this. It turns the verb into a naming word, puts in on the front and whose on the end, and says in her coming. And she is the one who comes: up to this verse she has been handed from one man to another as an object in a sentence, and here she arrives under her own verb. Third, and worth carrying hardest: and she urged him is the first verb in the whole book with a woman behind it. Fourth, that verb is strong — not asked and not suggested, but the word for egging somebody on, stirring them to do a thing they were not going to do, and elsewhere in the Bible it is usually a push toward something bad. Here it is a young woman getting more land out of her father, and the Bible uses the hard word without apologising for her. Who she urged is argued over, because Hebrew only says him; most take it to be her new husband, who is then to do the asking. Fifth, and worth carrying: the chapter turns back on itself. The very first thing in this book was that the sons of Israel asked — this same verb, its first appearance — asking God who should go up first. Now the word comes back for a girl asking her father for a piece of ground. It is the verb for asking and for requesting, one word for both, which is where the king called Saul got his name. Sixth, what she wants is a field: open country, ground you can plough, the word in the field where Cain killed his brother and the field Boaz owned. Not treasure, not jewellery. Land. Seventh, and worth carrying: getting down off the donkey is one of the rarest words in the Bible — three times in the whole of it, and all three times a woman getting off a donkey to ask a man for something. This verse, the same story in the book before, and years later Abigail sliding off hers in front of David. Hebrew seems to have kept one special word for exactly that movement. Eighth, a donkey is what people rode in peacetime and what carried the sacks, while a horse in these books nearly always means war. So she came out on the ordinary animal and got off it on purpose, which in that country was how you showed you were serious. Ninth, a run has just broken: up to now every voice in this chapter spoke once and never again — the people, God, Judah, a Canaanite king, Caleb. Here Caleb speaks a second time, the first person in the book to do so, twice out of six speeches, and both times handing something over. It is also the first time in the book anybody has spoken to a woman. Tenth, and worth carrying: the question is two little words with no verb in them at all — what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter, or what is it to you; the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father watching his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him, knowing perfectly well that something is coming. It is the chapter's second question, and the first one was put to God.  {"list":[{"chapter_code":"JDG01","exceeding":[{"verses":"14","findings":[{"word":"לָּֽךְ׃","parsing":"Preposition | second person feminine singular","term":"perfect","elsewhere":[],"explain":"The small joining word meaning to, or for, with an ending meaning you, where you are a woman. Wilt thou. And the whole question is two little words with no verb in them at all: what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter with you, or what is it to you — the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father seeing his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him and knowing perfectly well that something is coming. Ten things worth carrying out of this verse. First, the verse opens with the same word this book opened with — and it was, after the death of Joshua — which Hebrew uses as a doorway into a scene. There is no it in the Hebrew at all; the verb stands by itself and what follows is what was. Second, and worth carrying: Hebrew has no when-word for a thing like this. It turns the verb into a naming word, puts in on the front and whose on the end, and says in her coming. And she is the one who comes: up to this verse she has been handed from one man to another as an object in a sentence, and here she arrives under her own verb. Third, and worth carrying hardest: and she urged him is the first verb in the whole book with a woman behind it. Fourth, that verb is strong — not asked and not suggested, but the word for egging somebody on, stirring them to do a thing they were not going to do, and elsewhere in the Bible it is usually a push toward something bad. Here it is a young woman getting more land out of her father, and the Bible uses the hard word without apologising for her. Who she urged is argued over, because Hebrew only says him; most take it to be her new husband, who is then to do the asking. Fifth, and worth carrying: the chapter turns back on itself. The very first thing in this book was that the sons of Israel asked — this same verb, its first appearance — asking God who should go up first. Now the word comes back for a girl asking her father for a piece of ground. It is the verb for asking and for requesting, one word for both, which is where the king called Saul got his name. Sixth, what she wants is a field: open country, ground you can plough, the word in the field where Cain killed his brother and the field Boaz owned. Not treasure, not jewellery. Land. Seventh, and worth carrying: getting down off the donkey is one of the rarest words in the Bible — three times in the whole of it, and all three times a woman getting off a donkey to ask a man for something. This verse, the same story in the book before, and years later Abigail sliding off hers in front of David. Hebrew seems to have kept one special word for exactly that movement. Eighth, a donkey is what people rode in peacetime and what carried the sacks, while a horse in these books nearly always means war. So she came out on the ordinary animal and got off it on purpose, which in that country was how you showed you were serious. Ninth, a run has just broken: up to now every voice in this chapter spoke once and never again — the people, God, Judah, a Canaanite king, Caleb. Here Caleb speaks a second time, the first person in the book to do so, twice out of six speeches, and both times handing something over. It is also the first time in the book anybody has spoken to a woman. Tenth, and worth carrying: the question is two little words with no verb in them at all — what to you? Hebrew asks that way, and it can mean what do you want, or what is the matter, or what is it to you; the tone is left entirely to the moment. Here it is a father watching his daughter climb down off a donkey in front of him, knowing perfectly well that something is coming. It is the chapter's second question, and the first one was put to God.
